newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK sees China-Taiwan shipping ties impact minimal.
newsitem.headline: HK sees China-Taiwan shipping ties impact minimal.

text.p: The imminent start-up of direct shipping links between China and Taiwan will have minimal impact on Hong Kong's shipping business, government and shipping sources said on Tuesday.

"Our understanding is that they will only allow transshipment through Kaoshiung and will not allow direct imports to Taiwan, so the impact will be very minimal," said Richard Yuen, secretary of the Port Development Board.

Taipei said earlier this month the first direct sailings across the Taiwan Strait since 1949, linking Taiwan's southern port of Kaohsiung and Xiamen city in mainland China's Fujian province, could take place this week.

Taipei referred to the service as "offshore transshipment" rather than direct shipping because mainland cargoes would not be allowed to enter Taiwan proper but only a transshipment area in Kaohsiung port.
"People are getting excited as the date comes closer but actually the immediate impact is very limited," said Jensen Chow, a shipping analyst at ING Barings.

Most trade between China and Taiwan currently passes through third countries, usually Hong Kong, because Taipei has banned direct links with the mainland since the end of the Chinese civil war in 1949.
Yuen said the government had no figure on the volume of trade that might be affected by the transshipment sailings between the two shores because the number was too small.
Only cargoes heading for the United States from Xiamen or vice-versa would benefit since it would be closer and cheaper to transship them in Kaohsiung.
"Xiamen handled a total of 400,000 containers last year. If half of them went to the U.S. then roughly only 200,000 containers would be affected," Yuen said.
This compared with 13.3 million TEUs (20-foot equivalent units of containers) handled by Hong Kong last year.
Hong Kong's container transshipment handlers were also likely to take measures to meet competition from Kaohsiung, so the overall impact was difficult to estimate, he added.
But ING's Chow said it was possible that the start of transshipment sailings between China and Taiwan could eventually lead to real direct shipping links between the two shores soon.
"That's why the issue attracted the media's attention and caused investors concern," she said, adding that further analysis of the longer-term implications was necessary.

But Yuen said even if there were direct links between China and Taiwan it would not affect Hong Kong in a big way since only about eight percent, or one million containers, of Hong Kong's total throughput last year was China-Taiwan related.
"Even if the two sides can directly import and export containers, not all the one million boxes would be gone from Hong Kong," he added.

Since much of the trade was between Taiwan and points in China's Pearl River Delta such as Dongguan and Shenzhen, which are near Hong Kong, most goods were unlikely to be transported to Xiamen for shipment to Taiwan.

In 1995, when the board made a long-term throughput forecast to map out Hong Kong's container port development, it took into account the possibility of direct cross-straits shipping by stripping out the one million containers that would be affected.
Even then, the board predicted eight percent growth in container throughput for Hong Kong this year.
"So their (China-Taiwan containers) continued passage through Hong Kong is a bonus," Yuen said. -- Hong Kong News Room (852) 2843 6369
